Gaps (evidence-linked), grounded in what we have:
G1: No clause-level versioned regulatory retrieval benchmark with in-force labels and version-selection metrics. Evidence: arxiv:2605.23497 (312 synthetic German QA pairs, end-answer judge only, no retrieval metrics — C004, C007/C019); doi:10.1145/3589335.3651895 (QA benchmark, no version overlap — analysis); TempRALM reports recall@k of gold passage but on Wikipedia/tennis, no version-level in-force labels (arxiv:2401.13222, C017). research_question: build benchmark. confidence high. verification_required: search recent 2024-2026 benchmarks for point-in-time legal retrieval / statutory version retrieval; check EU/UK and US (e.g., "as-of" date retrieval) — but search budget exhausted; note.

G2: Soft temporal weighting versus hard validity-interval filtering have never been compared head-to-head, and the temporal weight is tuned without leakage control. G3: No retrieval-agnostic validation across retriever families; TempRALM instantiates one retriever (Atlas/Contriever) yet claims retrieval-agnosticism. Evidence C001, C017, analysis. confidence medium.

Modifications (2-5), with strongest recommended:
M1: Validity-interval-aware temporal score (in-force indicator / piecewise) replacing monotone elapsed-time decay; retrieval-agnostic. Differs from TempRALM (distance decay) and from hard filter (continuous, but interval-conditioned); expected benefit: aligns the score with legal applicability, should dominate both on historical queries. Novelty hedged: combination of interval-aware score within a retrieval-agnostic re-ranker appears unpublished among retrieved work. Difficulty: implementation moderate (needs in-force intervals), experimental moderate.
M2: Leakage-controlled evaluation protocol as contribution (held-out lambda tuning, timestamp-shuffled and date-offset controls, content-blind date-only baseline). Difficulty low implementation, moderate experimental.
M3: Regime-conditioned temporal weighting (query-date regime classifier/adjustment) to avoid recency bias. Differs from single global decay. Difficulty moderate/high.
M4: Clause-level versioned benchmark with version-selection metrics (in-force accuracy@k) and cross-retriever arms. Differs from Prior et al.'s end-answer-only benchmark. Difficulty high implementation, high experimental.

input.gap: No public benchmark evaluates retrieval over overlapping successive regulatory revisions with per-passage version labels and an in-force ground truth. Existing resources either score end answers on synthetic statutory questions (arxiv:2605.23497), measure gold-passage recall on Wikipedia/tennis versions (arxiv:2401.13222), or test temporal QA over non-versioned snippets (doi:10.1145/3589335.3651895).
input.potential_experiment: Build a clause-level benchmark from amended statutes with archived version snapshots, per-version effective/expiry dates and time-stamped queries, and report version-selection accuracy@k (fraction of top-k passages from the in-force version) alongside end-answer accuracy, stratified by current versus historical query regime.
input.research_question: Can a clause-level benchmark of overlapping regulatory revisions with version labels and in-force ground truth be constructed such that retrieval-layer version-selection accuracy can be measured separately from answer accuracy?
input.verification_required: A broader search of 2024-2026 legal-IR and temporal-retrieval venues for point-in-time or as-of-date statutory retrieval datasets is still required; the present search budget is exhausted and Semantic Scholar was intermittently unavailable, so the absence of such a benchmark is a bounded negative finding.
input.why_unaddressed: The retrieved benchmarks were designed for different units of analysis: Prior et al. label QA pairs by the version required to answer but evaluate only generated answers with an LLM judge and report no retrieval metrics, while TempRALM evaluates gold-passage recall in a Wikipedia setting without legal validity intervals. No retrieved work labels both retrieval candidates by version validity and queries by target date in a regulatory corpus.

take into account the temporal validity of a statute as a hard constraint

By injecting synthetic publication dates into candidate passages while keeping their content unchanged, Fang et al. show that documents labeled as more recent are systematically promoted in the ranking

input.gap: Soft temporal score fusion and hard validity-interval filtering have never been compared under identical corpora, retrievers and tuning conditions, and the temporal weight has never been selected with leakage controls. TempRALM tunes its scaling factor for relative importance with no reported held-out split, while Prior et al. evaluate only a hard filter and report no soft re-ranking arm.
input.potential_experiment: A leakage-controlled head-to-head study: identical index and top-k; arms for semantic-only, future-mask-only, recency-only, soft elapsed-time decay, hard in-force filtering and an oracle filter; lambda tuned on a held-out question split; controls that shuffle version timestamps and shift query dates; results reported per query-date regime.
input.research_question: Under leakage-controlled tuning, does a soft temporal score add any version-selection or answer-accuracy benefit over hard in-force filtering and over a timestamp-shuffled control?
input.verification_required: Requires executing the recorded experiment plan E001 and verifying its runs; no published result currently settles it.
input.why_unaddressed: The two lines of work are disjoint in the retrieved literature: the soft-score paper is evaluated on web/Wikipedia content without validity intervals and without a hard-filter baseline, and the hard-filter paper is evaluated on statutory QA without any soft re-ranking arm or retrieval metrics. Neither reports a leakage control for the temporal weight even though date injection alone is shown to shift rankings.

evidence.quote: our approach could be used to extend any retriever that ranks documents using a numerical similarity score between a query and a document corpus
The TempRALM retriever uses the standard Atlas-large

input.research_question: Is the effect of a temporal re-ranking wrapper stable across sparse and dense retrievers under matched budgets, or specific to one embedding space?
input.verification_required: Requires the cross-retriever experiment; also a search for retriever-agnostic temporal wrappers in other domains.
input.why_unaddressed: Retrieval-agnosticism is stated as a design property rather than tested as an empirical claim, and the only instantiation reported is a single dense retriever on a non-legal corpus.

M1:
title: "Validity-interval-aware temporal score instead of monotone elapsed-time decay"
description: Replace f(|t_q - t_v|) with an interval-aware term w(p) = 1 if t_q in [effective(p), expiry(p)), else a bounded penalty, optionally combined with a graded proximity term inside the in-force set. Retrieval-agnostic: still a scalar added to s(q,p).
why_differs: TempRALM uses reciprocal/exponential distance decay (monotone, nearest version wins) with no validity intervals; Prior et al./TaxFlow use a binary hard filter that discards all out-of-force versions entirely. This keeps a continuous, differentiable-ish score but conditions on the legal relation (in-force interval) rather than distance.
technical_mechanism: score = s(q,p) + lambda * g(t_q, interval(p)) where g is a step (in-force indicator) or a piecewise function: +1 if in force, small negative or zero otherwise, optionally plus mu * f(|t_q - t_v|) restricted to the in-force set; intervals from effective/expiry dates.
expected_benefit: Removes the technical invalidity (C010), should dominate monotone decay on historically anchored queries and match hard filtering while allowing graded preference among simultaneously valid versions.

input.description: Replace the monotone elapsed-time decay f(|t_q - t_v(p)|) with a validity-interval-aware temporal term g(t_q, interval(p)). The temporal component returns a large bonus exactly when t_q lies inside the passage version's in-force interval and a small or zero value otherwise, optionally adding a weak proximity term m * f(|t_q - t_v|) restricted to the in-force set so that simultaneously valid versions can still be distinguished by relevance to the query date. The wrapper remains a scalar addition to s(q,p) applied at re-ranking time with no re-indexing.
input.expected_benefit: Removes the technical mismatch between elapsed time and legal applicability: it cannot favour a temporally near but out-of-force version, so it should match or exceed hard filtering on current-version queries while avoiding the recency-bias failure on historically anchored queries that a monotone decay is prone to.
input.experimental_difficulty_basis: Needs the same versioned corpus and held-out tuning effort as the original plan, plus per-regime reporting; no new model training or index rebuild is required, so the incremental experimental cost over the base plan is limited to extra arms and interval metadata handling.
input.implementation_difficulty_basis: The scoring change is a few lines, but it requires effective/expiry dates at passage granularity, which must be curated or extracted from consolidated statute data; without that metadata the variant cannot be instantiated.
input.main_risk: If every query maps to a single unambiguous in-force version, the interval-aware term degenerates into hard filtering and contributes nothing beyond it; the graded proximity component may then be the only differentiator.
input.potential_novelty: Hedged: no retrieved work combines an interval-aware temporal term with a retrieval-agnostic re-ranking wrapper, but this is a bounded negative finding because the paper search budget was exhausted and TempRALM could not be citation-expanded through OpenAlex. The novelty claim is therefore provisional.
input.technical_mechanism: score(q,p) = s(q,p) + lambda * g(t_q, interval(p)), where interval(p) = [effective(p), expiry(p)) and g is a step function equal to 1 when t_q is in force and 0 or a small negative otherwise; a second variant uses g = 1_inforce + mu * f(|t_q - t_v(p)|) to keep graded preference among in-force versions.
input.title: Validity-interval-aware temporal scoring instead of monotone elapsed-time decay
input.why_differs: TempRALM uses a reciprocal/exponential decay in the query-document time difference, which is monotone toward the temporally nearest version and has no notion of validity intervals. Prior et al. and TaxFlow use a hard filter that removes all out-of-force versions, giving no graded signal among simultaneously valid versions. This modification keeps the retrieval-agnostic soft score but conditions it on the legal validity relation rather than temporal distance.

input.description: Make the evaluation protocol itself a contribution: tune the temporal weight lambda only on a held-out question split; add controls that randomly permute version timestamps across candidate passages and that shift query dates by a fixed offset so elapsed-time order no longer aligns with in-force order; add a content-blind date-only ranker that scores passages using timestamps alone. Report the full lambda sensitivity curve rather than the argmax, and report version-selection accuracy and answer accuracy separately.
input.expected_benefit: Establishes whether any observed temporal gain is genuine retrieval skill or a timestamp shortcut; without it the hypothesis is not testable. A protocol of this kind is also reusable for any future versioned-document retrieval work.
input.experimental_difficulty_basis: The controls are cheap to implement and run, but they require a held-out split, a shuffled-timestamp corpus clone and careful per-regime reporting, which adds orchestration rather than new resources.
input.implementation_difficulty_basis: All components are simple data transformations and score re-computation on top of the existing pipeline; no modelling, index rebuild or extra data acquisition is needed.
input.main_risk: The protocol may show that the soft temporal term has no effect at all, which would be a scientifically useful but not a positive contribution on its own.
input.potential_novelty: Hedged: neither retrieved paper reports leakage controls for a temporal weight, but benchmark-methodology novelty is inherently weaker and reviewers may treat it as standard good practice rather than a contribution.
required_baselines: Shuffled-timestamp variant of every temporal arm
input.technical_mechanism: Data-level controls (permuted timestamps, shifted query dates) plus a date-only scoring arm; protocol-level control by tuning lambda on a held-out split and reporting the sensitivity curve instead of a single tuned value.
input.title: Leakage-controlled tuning and control-arm protocol for temporal re-ranking claims
input.why_differs: TempRALM selects its temporal scaling factor for relative importance with no reported held-out validation or content-blind control, and Prior et al. have no soft re-ranking arm to control at all. This modification makes explicit the controls that both lines of work leave implicit.

input.description: Condition the temporal component on the query's date regime instead of using one global weight. Current/post-amendment queries use the standard forward-looking adjustment (prefer the version in force at t_q), while historically anchored queries use a backward-anchored rule that prefers the version in force at t_q even when it is far in the past and never rewards recency. The regime can be inferred from the query's target date relative to the corpus history or from an explicit as-of date extraction.
input.expected_benefit: Addresses the opposite-direction tension between current and historical queries, which a single monotone decay cannot satisfy; should retain post-amendment gains while removing recency-bias degradation.
input.experimental_difficulty_basis: Requires per-regime evaluation which the plan already includes, and a rule for regime assignment that must itself be validated with an ablation; no additional heavy computation.
input.implementation_difficulty_basis: Needs a regime-classification or date-extraction step and two weight sets, plus validation that the regime signal is available at deployment time.
input.main_risk: If the query target date is not reliably inferable in deployment, regime-conditioning is unusable and the added complexity has no practical payoff.
input.potential_novelty: Hedged: the retrieved literature motivates the two regimes but proposes no regime-conditioned temporal score; with the search budget exhausted this is a provisional assessment.
input.technical_mechanism: Two separate temporal weight sets (or an asymmetric function) selected by an inferred query regime, with the historical branch anchored on the in-force version at t_q rather than on the newest version.
input.title: Regime-conditioned temporal weighting for current versus historically anchored queries
input.why_differs: A single global elapsed-time decay treats all queries identically, whereas Prior et al. show that recency helps post-cutoff queries but produces a documented recency bias on historically anchored ones; TempRALM has no mechanism for this distinction.

input.description: Build and release a clause-level benchmark of overlapping successive revisions from an amended regulatory corpus: archived version snapshots, per-clause effective and expiry dates, time-stamped queries with target dates, gold in-force version labels per query, and published retrieval-layer metrics (version-selection accuracy@k, Recall@k, MRR, nDCG@k) alongside end-answer accuracy. Include arms using BM25 and at least two dense encoders under matched segmentation and top-k to test the retrieval-agnosticism claim.
input.expected_benefit: Supplies the missing measurement instrument for the whole line of work, makes version-selection accuracy comparable across methods, and allows the retrieval-agnosticism claim to be tested rather than asserted.
input.experimental_difficulty_basis: Requires curating version history and validity intervals, query construction with expert checking, and cross-retriever runs; the effort is dominated by data curation and annotation rather than compute.
input.implementation_difficulty_basis: Amended statute corpora are large and versioning metadata is often incomplete; clause-level alignment across versions and effective/expiry dates must be reconstructed, and exact reproduction requires archiving snapshots because legislation changes.
input.main_risk: High curation cost with construct-validity risk: if queries are synthesised by an LLM, measured gains may not transfer to real legal queries, and a small benchmark limits statistical power for per-regime analysis.
input.potential_novelty: Hedged: no retrieved resource provides clause-level overlapping revisions with in-force labels and retrieval metrics, but this is a bounded negative finding since the search budget was exhausted and some venues were unreachable.
input.technical_mechanism: Corpus construction pipeline that snapshots statute versions, aligns clauses across amendments, records effective/expiry dates, and derives per-passage version labels used to compute version-selection accuracy at query target dates.
input.title: Clause-level versioned-revision benchmark with version-selection metrics and cross-retriever arms
input.why_differs: Prior et al.'s benchmark is evaluated only through LLM-judged end answers with no retrieval metrics and no per-passage version labels, TIQ tests temporal reasoning over non-versioned snippets, and TempRALM evaluates gold-passage recall on Wikipedia rather than regulatory amendments.

input.direction: Change the temporal component from a monotone elapsed-time decay to a validity-interval-aware, retrieval-agnostic re-ranking term, and make the leakage-controlled evaluation protocol and a clause-level versioned benchmark part of the contribution rather than only the evaluation. Concretely: score(q,p) = s(q,p) + lambda * g(t_q, interval(p)) where g is governed by the version's in-force interval, with hard in-force filtering, monotone decay and a content-blind date-only ranker as baselines, lambda tuned on a held-out split, and version-selection accuracy@k reported per query-date regime across BM25 and dense retrievers.
input.hypothesis: A retrieval-agnostic temporal re-ranking term conditioned on a passage version's in-force interval rather than on elapsed time improves version-selection accuracy and answer accuracy on time-stamped regulatory queries relative to semantic-only retrieval and to monotone elapsed-time decay, matches hard in-force filtering where the latter is applicable, and does so robustly across sparse and dense retrievers when the temporal weight is selected on held-out data with timestamp-shuffled and date-offset controls.
input.rationale: The evidence does not support continuing with the original mechanism as stated. TempRALM already publishes the retrieval-agnostic addition of an elapsed-time temporal term to a retriever's semantic score, including future-passage masking (C001, C003, C005), so the mechanism is pre-empted. More importantly, elapsed time is not the legal validity relation: TempRALM's score is monotone in the time difference (C008) while legal applicability is determined by effective/amendment dates, and Prior et al. conclude temporal validity must be a hard constraint (C002, C010). The empirical case is also unguarded: TempRALM tunes its temporal scaling factor without a held-out split or leakage control (C014) even though date injection alone is reported to reorder rankings with content held fixed (C016), so any soft-term accuracy gain would be uninterpretable as temporal skill (U007, C018). The surviving, evidence-backed opening is therefore neither the original decay term nor a repeat of hard filtering, but an interval-aware soft score that keeps the retrieval-agnostic framing while conditioning on the property that actually determines applicability, tested under a leakage-controlled protocol and measured with version-selection accuracy on a clause-level versioned corpus, which no retrieved resource provides (G001-G004, C019). This deserves investigation next because it is the only variant that simultaneously addresses the pre-emption (novelty), the proxy invalidity (technical validity) and the leakage confounder (experimental validity), and because the interval-aware soft score may recover graded behaviour (including among simultaneously valid versions) that a binary filter cannot express; the degeneracy risk is recorded as U011.
